Context

Stop 5 came with something none of the previous stops offered: a conversation with the owner. He met me at the store, walked me through his philosophy, and was candid about the constraints and choices that shape the product. That kind of transparency is rare, and it informed how I read what followed.

I ordered the chicken shawarma, served on a tray with toum on the side, a bowl of pickles, and fries. The presentation is clean and deliberate. Hell's Shawarma is clearly a considered operation.

Meat
34 / 40

The first thing worth noting is the choice of chicken thighs over breasts — a decision the owner made deliberately for fat content and flavour. It is the right call. Thighs hold moisture better on a rotisserie and deliver more natural depth. The texture holds up well, and the juiciness is consistent throughout.

The issue lies in the marinade. The chicken arrives at a deep, saturated red — a signal of a heavily spiced, oil-rich blend that leans far from the lighter, more aromatic profiles typical of traditional Arabic shawarma. The marinade dominates rather than complements, pushing the natural flavour of the meat into the background. The excess oil — noticeable enough to drip — confirmed this was a marinade-heavy approach rather than a restraint-first one.

That said, the thigh choice cushions the blow significantly. What you lose in marinade subtlety, you recover in texture and mouthfeel. Solidly decent.

Flavour & Seasoning 17/20Juiciness & Texture 14/15Freshness 3/5
Sauce
18 / 20

The toum is homemade. In Colombo, that alone is worth acknowledging. The colour is right, the consistency is right, and — critically — it is not mayo-based. These are not small things. Most of what passes for toum in this city is diluted with mayonnaise to cut cost and effort. This is not that.

What holds it back is garlic intensity. The punch is dialed back compared to the better toums available in the city, suggesting either a conservative garlic ratio or a slightly imperfect emulsification. The texture leans denser than ideally aerated. Solid, but not yet assertive enough to be a standout.

Flavour & Authenticity 14/15Integration 4/5
Assembly
9 / 10

The meat-to-bread ratio comes in at 47.5% — the highest recorded in this series so far, and technically deserving of more than the 5/5 the scale allows.

Distribution, however, is uneven. The filling concentrates along one side, creating inconsistent bites. The pickles, while present, are sliced far too thinly to register meaningfully. With a marinade this heavy and a toum this mild, a sharp, punchy pickle could have done significant work here.

Meat/Bread Ratio 5/5Distribution 4/5
Bread
6 / 10

Custom-made for the restaurant — and the owner was candid about why it falls short of what you would find in the Middle East. Authentic Arabic flatbread requires specific machinery that simply is not available in Sri Lanka.

The bread shows some browning and grill marks, but stops short of developing any meaningful crispness. More problematically, it is noticeably thin — it could not adequately contain the oil dripping from the filling, and there was a chalky, dusty residue on the surface on contact.

Texture & Freshness 3/5Structural Integrity 3/5
Value
17 / 20

At LKR 1,500, Hell's Shawarma sits in the middle of the price range encountered in this series. The portion is generous, the meat ratio leads the field, and the overall experience is comfortably above average.

The bread is the one area where the price is not fully earned — but given the context the owner provided around local sourcing constraints, it reads less as a shortcut and more as an honest limitation.

Context

Stop 4: Grillo's, a spot that comes highly recommended by Gulf kids in Colombo. First impressions were strong. The ambiance stands out, and the menu is easily the most extensive I have seen so far. I went straight for their best seller, the Toum Chicken Shawarma, and ordered two Regulars.

A side note on the "OG shawarma" — it comes with two types of meat, which felt a bit unconventional. Personally, I still lean towards toum with chicken or tahini/toum with beef if you are going for authenticity. Two proteins in one wrap muddies both.

Meat
22 / 40

The chicken ends up taking a back seat here, largely overwhelmed by the toum. The marinade does not align with a classic shawarma profile — the flavour notes feel slightly off. From the texture and cut, I hypothesised it was not shaved from a vertical rotisserie. Staff were not available for comment. Somewhat unfortunately, my takeaway shawarma included a small bone, which confirmed my suspicions.

The meat was reasonably juicy and the texture held up decently — but the flavour foundation was not strong enough to carry the wrap on its own.

Flavour & Seasoning 11/20Juiciness & Texture 8/15Freshness 3/5
Sauce
17 / 20

A generous amount of toum is used, which works in its favour. It overpowered the meat — but given the subpar meat, I hold the meat responsible rather than the sauce. The garlic flavour is strong and delivers, making it one of the better toums I have had in this series so far.

That said, the texture leans noticeably dense rather than light and aerated, suggesting an imperfect emulsion or perhaps insufficient egg whites. Solid overall, but not quite technically refined.

Flavour & Authenticity 12/15Integration 5/5
Assembly
7 / 10

The wrap suffers from poor distribution, with most of the filling concentrated along one side rather than evenly layered throughout. This led to inconsistent bites — some overloaded, others feeling lacking. The meat-to-bread ratio was bordering 0.4, so it scores well on that front.

Meat/Bread Ratio 4/5Distribution 3/5
Bread
8 / 10

The bread is lightly grilled but stops short of developing any real crispness — which I am perfectly fine with. It does the job, and given the horror shows I have seen so far in this series, I feel like I should commend them for this.

Texture & Freshness 4/5Structural Integrity 4/5
Value
11 / 20

At LKR 1,925, this is the most expensive shawarma I have tasted so far. The value-for-money score is noticeably dragging the final rating. Arabian Knights, a competitor with a similar cost structure, will serve as the benchmark going forward.

Context

My third stop took me to Arabian Knights (another spot recommended on Reddit). I arrived just after their Iftar promotion ended and was seated immediately.

The menu was fairly extensive, so I asked the staff what went into their "Dubai Style" shawarma. I was told it came with "two sauces and coleslaw." Knowing that combination would likely tank the authenticity score, I asked for something simpler. The closest option was the "Lite," which I was told was meant for kids. Still, it had the basics: sauce, meat, and pickles, with no fries. Good enough.

Meat
19 / 40

I received both shawarmas in under six minutes, which immediately made me suspect the meat had already been sliced and was sitting on the grill rather than being shaved fresh off the rotisserie. The chicken wasn't juicy and tasted quite bland, lacking the depth of seasoning you'd expect from good shawarma. There were a few charred bits scattered throughout the wrap — and not the kind of char that's good.

Flavour & Seasoning 11/20Juiciness & Texture 6/15Freshness 2/5
Sauce
13 / 20

The sauce leaned noticeably yellow, which suggests it was likely a mayonnaise-based garlic sauce rather than traditional toum. The flavour profile felt more sweet and lacked the garlic punch I was expecting. I noticed some reviews complaining about the overuse of the "toum", but I thought it was an appropriate amount — with an appropriate amount of spillage with every bite.

Flavour & Authenticity 8/15Integration 5/5
Assembly
6 / 10

No fries, and only a singular pickle included. The meat-to-bread ratio and distribution were both middling — there was no real generosity to the filling, and the overall balance felt like a miniaturised shawarma rather than a complete one.

Meat/Bread Ratio 3/5Distribution 3/5
Bread
6 / 10

Structural integrity held up reasonably well, but the texture and freshness left something to be desired. The bread did not arrive particularly warm and lacked the char or crispness that would have elevated it.

Texture & Freshness 2/5Structural Integrity 4/5
Value
11 / 20

At LKR 1,843 all-in, this is among the pricier stops in the series. Given what was on the plate — no fries, a single pickle, middling meat — the price is difficult to justify. The "Lite" framing does not help: it was designed for kids, and it was priced for adults.

Context

By popular demand, my second stop was Bamba Food Square, on a mission to see if Le Beirut lived up to its name. The Square buzzed with great ambience and plenty of stalls, but I only had one goal in mind.

The "Authentic Shawarma" did not come with fries (criminal), so I went for the mispelt "Fries Shwarma" instead. Too late to turn back now. The staff patiently walked us through the options, and it arrived neatly presented on a wooden board with sides of toum and kochichi sauce (?).

Meat
20 / 40

The marinated chicken thighs were sliced after cooking rather than shaved directly from a vertical rotisserie. Because the pieces were cut thicker, each bite contained a higher proportion of interior meat and comparatively less surface-area exposure to Maillard browning. Thicker cuts resulted in a more uniform, less texturally varied chew, with fewer charred edges throughout. The seasoning had a curry-leaning profile, though I'm not knowledgeable enough to identify the exact spice responsible (too much cumin?).

Flavour & Seasoning 11/20Juiciness & Texture 6/15Freshness 3/5
Sauce
14 / 20

The toum had good flavour authenticity, but its integration into the wrap was uneven. Although the quantity seemed adequate during assembly, much of it concentrated toward the edges, leading to inconsistent bites — meaning I had to compensate by using the additional dip. I sampled the kochichi sauce, but it was far too overpowering unless it was intended to be mixed with the toum (ruining the best condiment ever created).

Flavour & Authenticity 12/15Integration 2/5
Assembly
9 / 10

I appreciated them adhering to the core components without any superfluous additions. Pickles were sliced into coins rather than strips, which led to occasional bursts of acidity rather than the usual even distribution. The thicker-cut fries (more akin to wedges) were an interesting choice, but did not earn any brownie points from me.

Meat/Bread Ratio 5/5Distribution 4/5
Bread
9 / 10

A brown sauce was applied directly to the pita before being grilled closed, creating a well-sealed structure and a crisp exterior. Shawarma was received warm and crispy with an appropriate amount of charring — no complaints here! Excellent meat/bread ratio as well!

Texture & Freshness 4/5Structural Integrity 5/5
Value
16 / 20

Rs.1,300 base with a Rs.200 add-on for fries seems reasonable assuming it did not occupy volume that would have otherwise been allocated to the toum. Dinemore's Rs.1,150 price point offers a restaurant setting but their scale and centralised supply chain offers stronger economies of scale, making the price comparison imperfect against a food square stall. They are competitively priced for the format, but not a price leader in the market.

Portion Size vs Cost 16/20
Verdict

A proper vertical rotisserie would bring them closer to true shawarma authenticity. Even small tweaks like better toum integration could lift the overall score, assuming fixed pricing. Some reviews correctly question the authenticity, yet a 4.4 rating suggests many customers are perfectly happy with the status quo, so perhaps change isn't necessary for the local market.

Despite the welcoming service and pleasant ambience, it ultimately falls short of retaining this shawarma purist.

Context

I'll admit I didn't come in with high expectations. I had tried several "authentic" shawarma spots in Colombo before starting this series, and Dinemore didn't register as a serious contender. I was wrong.

Meat
27 / 40

The flavour and seasoning of the freshly carved chicken were decent, though somewhat muted. Chicken was sufficiently warm when consumed. Some shavings were slightly tougher, but the majority were reasonably juicy. I did not encounter much edge caramelisation from the vertical rotisserie (which usually adds character). A noticeable amount of grease transfer to my notebook pages which is a good sign (less so for my cut).

Flavour & Seasoning 14/20Juiciness & Texture 10/15Freshness 3/5
Sauce
13 / 20

The toum lacked the sharp, tangy acid balance it typically has, but still tasted very good. It was heavily integrated into the wrap, which slightly muted the meat seasoning. I appreciate them for not trying to reinvent the wheel with the sauce.

Flavour & Authenticity 10/15Integration 3/5
Assembly
9 / 10

Very generous meat to bread ratio. Additional ingredients played a subtle role and did not overpower the overall balance. Fries were integrated Lebanese-style into the wrap, though lacking crisp edges.

Meat/Bread Ratio 5/5Distribution 4/5
Bread
5 / 10

Not the bread I'm used to. This could be a cultural adaptation. The bread showed some griddle charring but was not served warm when dining in. The outer layer of the flatbread was peeling slightly. The interior surface was heavily saturated with sauce, likely due to either excessive toum application, a thin flatbread base, or both. Despite the generous serving, the contents were not overflowing. This was a genuine concern since my takeaway shawarma was rubber banded.

Texture & Freshness 2/5Structural Integrity 3/5
Value
20 / 20

In my prime, I could eat more shawarma, but two shawarma sufficiently filled me up this time. For a full meal and 52g of protein at LKR 2,300 (inc. tax), this is unbeatable.

Portion Size vs Cost 20/20
Verdict

Dinemore has quietly built something consistent over the years. In many ways, it feels like an unsung hero in Sri Lanka's shawarma space.

This was a competent shawarma with clear strengths yet noticeable flaws. The meat-to-bread ratio and overall value stand out positively. Their slogan, "So much for so little", is justified. At this price point, it's difficult to argue against it.

How it works

The Approach

I'm a bit of a quant at heart, so each shawarma is scored out of 100 by weighting subjective and objective elements into a single score.

For consistency, I'll buy two chicken shawarmas: one eaten fresh and one taken home to dissect properly. For now, I'll be focusing on chicken shawarma and later expanding into beef, sarook, and other variants (not extra spicy chilli Mexican shawarma).

Interpreting the Score

These ranges are deliberately wide. Most shawarma lives in the middle as truly great ones are rare.

ScoreComment
90+Genuinely excellent and memorable.
80–89Solid and worth going back for
70–79Okay, but clearly flawed
60–69Decent, but something is noticeably off
<60Not for me

Closing Remarks

This is the system I'll be using for every review going forward.

You're free to agree, disagree, or ignore the score entirely. It's simply a way of keeping comparisons honest and repeatable.

If anyone has any recommendations on places to visit, please feel free to reach out!

That's a wrap!

About

Why I Started This

I've travelled all over the world, and wherever I go, I usually end up looking for shawarma (or at least the closest local equivalent).

I'm currently on vacation and I thought it might be fun to actually start writing this stuff down.

This page is really just for fun, curiosity, and people who genuinely love shawarma.

The Reference Point

I spent most of my life growing up and working in the Middle East, and that's shaped how I think shawarma should taste.

I'm still chasing the nostalgia of that first bite of Mama Noura's and pre-COVID Laffah.

That style is the reference point I'll be using. Not because it's the only way, but because it's the one I know best.

Some Caveats

Taste is subjective and I'm fully aware of that. I'm mostly rating authenticity, but I'll be flexible when it comes to cultural adaptations.

I'm not trying to be one of those food critic pages where everything somehow scores above a 9/10.

My journey begins in a location that isn't known for shawarma, so early scores will be low. This is intentional and will keep the scale meaningful.
